internship.title: Cybersecurity Internship
internship.description: An industry-oriented defensive cybersecurity internship designed around progressive analyst work rather than a renamed course. The program develops security foundations, network and endpoint analysis, authorized vulnerability assessment, web/application security testing, identity and cryptographic controls, threat intelligence and detection engineering, incident response, digital-forensic reasoning, and secure engineering practices. Interns produce evidence-backed work products, complete module-level engineering tasks, maintain Git-based audit trails, and finish with one substantial defensive capstone: a local Security Operations Triage Toolkit. The program uses current authoritative references including NIST NICE, NIST CSF 2.0, NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, OWASP Top 10:2025/WSTG/ASVS, MITRE ATT&CK, Sigma, Zeek, Suricata, NVD, CISA KEV, and CIS Controls.
prerequisites: Basic command-line usage on Linux or another Unix-like system.
Basic computer networking concepts such as IP addresses, ports, DNS, and HTTP.
Basic Python or another scripting language is helpful but not mandatory before the first modules; Python is introduced as an engineering tool during the internship.
Ability to read structured text such as JSON and CSV.
A legal, controlled lab environment for active security testing.
objectives: Apply a structured security-risk vocabulary to technical findings.
Conduct authorized network discovery and interpret host/network telemetry.
Prioritize vulnerabilities using evidence, exposure, asset context, and authoritative vulnerability data.
Perform structured web-security testing in controlled environments using OWASP guidance.
Assess identity, privilege, secret handling, cryptographic purpose, and secure configuration controls.
Develop and tune defensive detections using ATT&CK-oriented reasoning, Sigma concepts, and network telemetry.
Conduct incident triage, evidence handling, timeline analysis, and recovery verification using current NIST guidance.
Build, test, document, and present a defensive security-triage application with explicit security boundaries and limitations.

modules.title: Cybersecurity Foundations, Ethics and Risk
modules.description: Establishes the operating model for the internship: authorized security work, risk language, asset awareness, evidence-driven decisions, professional documentation, and a repeatable requirement-to-remediation workflow. The work is framed around the NICE Framework and NIST CSF rather than a list of disconnected tools.
objectives: Explain confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, accountability, and least privilege in operational contexts.
Distinguish assets, threats, vulnerabilities, risks, controls, findings, incidents, and evidence.
Apply authorization boundaries and rules of engagement to practical security activity.
Create a small risk register and map findings to defensible security outcomes.
Use Git commits and security notes as auditable engineering evidence.

lessons.title: Security Principles and Risk Language
lessons.description: Builds a shared vocabulary for security work and shows how a technical weakness becomes a business risk only when context, likelihood, and impact are considered.
learningObjectives: Define key security principles and risk terms.
Separate a vulnerability from an exploit, threat, and incident.
Write risk statements that include affected asset, condition, consequence, and likelihood.

notes.text: From “bug” to “risk”

A vulnerability is a weakness; risk is a decision-relevant combination of uncertainty and consequence. Security work becomes useful when the analyst connects a technical observation to an affected asset, expected impact, existing controls, and a defensible prioritization rationale.

items: CIA is a security objective set, not a risk score by itself.
A control is not the same as evidence that the control works.
Severity labels should not replace context; an exposed development host and a crown-jewel identity system can carry very different business consequences.

notes.text: Do not invent impact, exploitability, or asset criticality values. State assumptions and identify what evidence is still needed.

quiz.question: Which statement best distinguishes a vulnerability from a risk?
options: A vulnerability is a weakness; risk incorporates uncertainty and potential consequence.
A vulnerability is always an incident.
A vulnerability and risk are identical terms.
quiz.answer: A vulnerability is a weakness; risk incorporates uncertainty and potential consequence.
quiz.explanation: The weakness is the vulnerability. Risk requires additional context about potential outcomes and uncertainty.

summary: Security analysis starts with assets and outcomes, not tools.
Risk statements should be evidence-based and explicit about assumptions.

lessons.title: Authorization, Ethics and Rules of Engagement
lessons.description: Turns legal/ethical boundaries into concrete operating constraints for labs, assessments, monitoring, and incident work.
learningObjectives: Define scope, authorization, and stop conditions.
Write a concise rules-of-engagement checklist.
Distinguish safe validation from uncontrolled exploitation.

notes.text: Authorized security testing requires explicit permission, a defined target boundary, safe handling of data, and a clear stop condition. In an internship setting, local VMs, deliberately vulnerable applications, and synthetic logs are preferred over public targets.

items: Identify systems and accounts in scope.
Identify techniques that are prohibited or require approval.
Define evidence handling and retention.
Define emergency contacts and stop conditions.
Record the test window and expected effect.
Never reuse credentials found during a lab on unrelated systems.
Do not scan third-party or public infrastructure merely because it is reachable.
Minimize collection: gather what is required to answer the security question and protect sensitive evidence.

quiz.question: What should exist before conducting an active scan against a system?
options: Explicit authorization and a defined scope
A request from an unrelated user
quiz.answer: Explicit authorization and a defined scope
quiz.explanation: Authorization and scope establish whether the activity is permitted and which systems are included.

summary: Scope and authorization are security controls.
A lab should have explicit boundaries before active testing begins.

lessons.title: Risk Register, Evidence and Git Workflow
lessons.description: Introduces the professional habit of recording findings, evidence, remediation ownership, and change history so another analyst can reproduce the reasoning.
learningObjectives: Create a concise security finding record.
Separate observation, evidence, analysis, recommendation, and owner.
Use Git branches and descriptive commits for security work.

notes.text: A useful finding record

items: Observation: what was seen.
Evidence: exact artifact, log, screenshot reference, command, or timestamp.
Analysis: why it matters and what is known versus assumed.
Recommendation: the smallest practical risk-reducing action.
Validation: how remediation will be confirmed.

notes.text:
git switch -c finding/weak-ssh-config
git add findings/ssh-config.md
git commit -m "Document SSH configuration finding"

items: Good security commits are specific enough to support review.
Do not put secrets, tokens, private keys, or personal data in Git history.
A finding without remediation verification is unfinished work.

quiz.question: Which artifact best proves that a finding was actually observed?
options: A precise evidence reference such as a log line or command result
A guess about likely attacker behavior
quiz.answer: A precise evidence reference such as a log line or command result
quiz.explanation: Evidence ties the finding to an observable artifact and allows review or reproduction.

summary: Evidence separates analysis from speculation.
Git is part of the security audit trail.

tasks.title: Build a Security Risk Register
tasks.description: Create a four-row risk register for a small lab environment using only evidence and explicit assumptions.
tasks.problemStatement: A lab contains a web VM, an analyst workstation, a log collector, and a test database. Create four defensible risk entries without inventing exploit results.
objectives: Record asset, threat, vulnerability/condition, impact, likelihood rationale, owner, and validation method.
Mark assumptions explicitly.
Keep risk language tied to the observed condition.
tasks.hint: Use one row per risk and separate what you observed from what you inferred.
tasks.solutionCode:
Asset,Condition,Impact,LikelihoodRationale,Recommendation,Validation
web-vm,Service exposed to lab network,Increases reachable attack surface,Exposure confirmed by local inventory,Restrict access to required hosts,Re-scan and verify firewall rule
log-collector,Logs lack synchronized timestamps,Weakens timeline correlation,Timestamp mismatch observed in sample logs,Configure time synchronization,Compare timestamps across two sources
test-db,Default sample credentials present in lab image,Unauthorized access could be attempted,Credential state verified during setup,Replace/remove sample credentials,Re-test authentication
analyst-workstation,Security artifacts stored without integrity metadata,Evidence tampering may be harder to detect,No hashes recorded in evidence folder,Hash exported artifacts,Recompute and compare SHA-256
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution keeps observations and validation steps explicit. A risk register is useful when each recommendation has an owner and a way to verify remediation.

deliverables: Risk register with four evidence-backed entries
Git history containing a clearly scoped change

modules.title: Network, Endpoint and Protocol Fundamentals
modules.description: Develops the practical foundation needed to interpret network connections and host telemetry before using higher-level security tooling. Interns learn how addresses, ports, DNS, HTTP(S), TLS, processes, users, and logs fit together.
objectives: Interpret IPv4 addressing, ports, TCP/UDP state, DNS resolution, HTTP methods/status, and TLS at an analyst level.
Use Linux commands to inspect listening services, routes, processes, and logs.
Recognize normal versus suspicious network behavior without assuming malice from a single event.
Explain why endpoint and network telemetry complement each other.

lessons.title: IP Addresses, Ports, TCP/UDP and Routing
lessons.description: Shows how network identities and connection states appear during triage and how to translate a packet-level observation into an analyst hypothesis.
learningObjectives: Interpret source/destination IP and port pairs.
Explain TCP connection establishment and why UDP behaves differently.
Use route and socket information to understand host connectivity.

notes.text: An IP address identifies a network endpoint in a particular context; a port identifies a service endpoint. A connection record is not proof of malicious activity. Analysts need context such as process ownership, expected service role, directionality, and timing.

ip addr
ip route
ss -lntup
ss -antup

items: Listening sockets tell you what a host is prepared to accept, not what a remote party will necessarily reach.
High-numbered source ports are commonly ephemeral client ports.
A single connection to a well-known port can be normal or malicious depending on the asset and process.

quiz.question: What does a TCP listening socket primarily indicate?
options: A local service is waiting for connection attempts
A remote attacker has already gained access
quiz.answer: A local service is waiting for connection attempts
quiz.explanation: A listening TCP socket represents a local service waiting for connection attempts; security interpretation requires context.

summary: Ports identify service endpoints within a transport protocol.
Socket inspection is useful for establishing a host baseline.

lessons.title: DNS, HTTP(S) and TLS for Analysts
lessons.description: Connects application-layer concepts to common telemetry such as DNS queries, HTTP request metadata, certificate information, and encrypted transport.
learningObjectives: Explain DNS query/response basics.
Interpret HTTP methods and response codes.
Explain what TLS protects and what remains observable without decryption.

notes.text: DNS translates names to addresses and provides a rich source of behavioral telemetry. HTTP exposes application metadata such as methods, hosts, paths, and status codes when the traffic is visible. TLS encrypts application data in transit and provides endpoint authentication when certificate validation succeeds; it does not make an endpoint invisible to network monitoring.

items: Repeated DNS failures can be misconfiguration, malware, or user error.
HTTP 401 and 403 reflect different authorization outcomes and should be interpreted in context.
Certificate metadata can help analysts identify unexpected services without decrypting payloads.

notes.text:
curl -I https://example.com
python -c "import socket; print(socket.getaddrinfo('example.com', 443))"

quiz.question: Which is the best interpretation of a TLS connection for a network defender?
options: Payload confidentiality is intended, but useful metadata can still exist
TLS proves the application is benign
quiz.answer: Payload confidentiality is intended, but useful metadata can still exist
quiz.explanation: TLS protects the application payload but does not eliminate metadata such as endpoints, timing, and certificate information.

summary: DNS and HTTP metadata are valuable telemetry.
TLS changes what can be observed, not whether observation is possible.

lessons.title: Linux and Windows Telemetry Basics
lessons.description: Introduces the host-side artifacts an analyst can use to validate network hypotheses, including processes, users, services, and event logs.
learningObjectives: Locate common Linux logs and process information.
Identify the purpose of Windows Event Logs at a high level.
Correlate a network event with a host process and account when telemetry allows it.

notes.text: Host telemetry provides the “who/what on the endpoint” context that network data often lacks. On Linux, process listings, socket ownership, authentication logs, and service managers can help. On Windows, Event Logs provide structured records across security, system, and application domains.

ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head
journalctl -n 50 --no-pager
systemctl --type=service --state=running | head -n 20

items: Do not treat every process with a network connection as malicious.
Authentication logs should be interpreted with account role, source location, and time-of-day context.
Preserve relevant timestamps and host identity when exporting evidence.

summary: Endpoint context helps validate network observations.
Log sources should be mapped to the security questions they can answer.

tasks.title: Create a Host Network Baseline
tasks.description: Collect and interpret the listening services and active connections on a Linux lab VM, then document expected services versus unexplained ones.
tasks.problemStatement: A new analyst receives a lab VM with several services. Produce a baseline that another analyst can compare against later.
objectives: Capture interfaces and routes.
List listening sockets with owning processes where available.
Record a baseline table with service, port, process, and expected purpose.
tasks.hint: Start with `ss -lntup` and inspect only the listeners that matter for the lab.
tasks.solutionCode:
ip addr
ip route
ss -lntup
ss -antup
tasks.solutionExplanation: These commands collect the minimum useful host-network evidence without modifying the machine. The analyst should then interpret each listener against the lab asset inventory.
constraints: Only the assigned lab VM may be inspected.

modules.title: Asset Discovery and Vulnerability Management
modules.description: Teaches the workflow from authorized discovery to vulnerability prioritization and remediation verification. Emphasis is placed on evidence, version/context checks, NVD/CVE data, CISA KEV prioritization, and remediation tracking.
objectives: Perform controlled discovery against explicitly authorized lab assets.
Differentiate service enumeration from vulnerability confirmation.
Interpret CVE/CWE/CVSS terminology and vendor evidence.
Use the CISA KEV catalog as a prioritization signal without treating it as the sole risk metric.
Write remediation and retest plans.

lessons.title: Authorized Discovery with Nmap
lessons.description: Builds a controlled reconnaissance workflow using a local lab target and shows how to record scan scope, options, and evidence.
learningObjectives: Explain host discovery, port scanning, service detection, and version detection.
Select a scan appropriate to a local lab question.
Record commands and target scope for reproducibility.

notes.text: Run active scans only against systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test. The practicals in this internship assume a private lab network.
nmap -sT -sV --version-light -oN scan.txt 192.168.56.101

A service/version scan identifies what the host appears to expose; it does not automatically prove a vulnerability. Version banners may be incomplete or misleading, so vulnerability confirmation requires additional evidence.

practicals.title: Controlled Service Inventory Scan
practicals.description: Run a TCP service inventory scan against the assigned local-lab VM and document the observed attack surface.
steps: Confirm the target IP is the assigned lab VM.
Run the scan with output saved to a file.
List each discovered port, service, and evidence source.
Identify one service that needs version confirmation.
practicals.output: A text report containing reachable TCP services and best-effort version information; exact ports depend on the lab VM state.

quiz.question: What is the safest interpretation of an Nmap service result?
options: It is evidence of an exposed service that needs context
It proves the version is exact
It proves a CVE is exploitable
quiz.answer: It is evidence of an exposed service that needs context
quiz.explanation: Scanning establishes observable exposure; vulnerability and exploitability require additional evidence.

summary: Reconnaissance is scoped, reproducible, and evidence-driven.
Service exposure is not equivalent to vulnerability confirmation.

lessons.title: CVE, CWE, CVSS, NVD and KEV
lessons.description: Provides a practical vulnerability-data model and teaches interns how to move from an identifier to a prioritization decision.
learningObjectives: Differentiate CVE, CWE, CVSS, and vendor advisory information.
Interpret a vulnerability record without overclaiming exploitability.
Use CISA KEV as one prioritization input.

notes.text: CVE names a publicly cataloged vulnerability. CWE describes weakness classes. CVSS is a scoring framework for vulnerability severity. The NVD aggregates standards-based vulnerability data and references. CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog identifies vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in the wild and can inform prioritization.

items: Do not infer exploitability from a CVSS score alone.
Check affected versions and vendor remediation guidance.
KEV status is a strong prioritization signal, but asset criticality and exposure still matter.

notes.text:
python - <<'PY'
import urllib.request
print(urllib.request.urlopen('https://nvd.nist.gov/', timeout=10).status)
PY

quiz.question: Which source is specifically described by CISA as its catalog of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild?
quiz.explanation: CISA maintains the KEV catalog for vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in the wild.

summary: Identifier, severity, exploitability, and organizational risk are different questions.
Use primary vulnerability records and vendor guidance before recommending remediation.

lessons.title: Remediation, Compensating Controls and Retesting
lessons.description: Turns vulnerability findings into actionable remediation work and a closed-loop validation plan.
learningObjectives: Write remediation options with owners and deadlines.
Distinguish remediation from compensating controls.
Design a retest that verifies the original condition is gone.

notes.text: A complete finding ends with a measurable remediation state. Updating software may remove a vulnerable version, while a network restriction may reduce exposure without removing the underlying weakness. The retest should reproduce the original observation at an appropriate level and verify that the relevant risk condition changed.

items: Restate the original evidence.
Choose remediation or a justified compensating control.
Define owner and target date.
Define acceptance criteria.
Retest using the same or stronger evidence method.
Record the closure evidence.

notes.text: Do not call a vulnerability “fixed” solely because a ticket was closed. Verification evidence is required.

summary: Remediation is a controlled change.
Closure requires evidence that the original risk condition has changed.

tasks.title: Prioritize a Vulnerability Queue
tasks.description: Triages a small queue of CVEs using asset criticality, exposure, vendor fix availability, and KEV presence.
tasks.problemStatement: Given a CSV of vulnerability records and a separate asset inventory, rank the work for the next remediation window without inventing exploit results.
objectives: Join vulnerability and asset data.
Elevate known-exploited items but retain asset context.
Produce a ranked queue with a written rationale.
requirements: CSV inputs containing vulnerability and asset metadata
tasks.hint: Use deterministic scoring rules and include a reason column so reviewers can challenge each decision.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The ranking is explainable and repeatable. KEV and internet exposure increase priority, while asset criticality keeps the decision tied to business context.
constraints: Use the supplied lab data only.
Do not state that a CVE was exploited unless the input data explicitly says so.

deliverables: Retest plan for the top finding

modules.title: Web and Application Security Testing
modules.description: Introduces structured web application assessment using the OWASP Top 10:2025, OWASP WSTG, and ASVS. Testing is performed only against local or explicitly authorized applications, with emphasis on validation and remediation rather than uncontrolled exploitation.
objectives: Explain major web application security risk categories in the current OWASP Top 10:2025.
Use an intercepting proxy or scanner responsibly in a lab.
Test input handling, authentication, authorization, session controls, and security configuration.
Write reproducible findings with safe proof and remediation advice.

lessons.title: OWASP Top 10:2025 and Secure Design
lessons.description: Maps application risk categories to practical review questions and emphasizes design defects over payload memorization.
learningObjectives: Identify the current OWASP Top 10:2025 categories.
Translate a category into review questions.
Explain why insecure design cannot be solved only by input filtering.

notes.text: OWASP Top 10:2025 lists Broken Access Control, Security Misconfiguration, Software Supply Chain Failures, Cryptographic Failures, Injection, Insecure Design, Authentication Failures, Software or Data Integrity Failures, Security Logging and Alerting Failures, and Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions.

items: Use the Top 10 as an awareness baseline, not a complete security specification.
ASVS provides more detailed verification requirements.
A design-level control can prevent entire classes of implementation mistakes.

quiz.question: Which OWASP Top 10:2025 category explicitly addresses missing or weak security telemetry and response signals?
options: A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures
quiz.answer: A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures
quiz.explanation: A09 covers situations where security-relevant activity is not logged or alerted effectively enough for detection and response.

summary: The 2025 Top 10 emphasizes root causes as well as symptoms.
ASVS complements the awareness-oriented Top 10 with verification requirements.

lessons.title: Intercepting Proxies and Safe Test Cases
lessons.description: Teaches the workflow of capturing a request, altering one controlled variable, observing the response, and recording evidence without destabilizing the lab application.
learningObjectives: Use Burp Suite or OWASP ZAP in a local lab.
Construct a minimal test case for authorization and input validation.
Distinguish a security finding from an expected application behavior.

notes.text: An intercepting proxy lets an analyst inspect and modify requests between a client and an authorized test application. The useful mindset is experimental: state the hypothesis, change one variable, observe the response, and preserve the evidence needed to reproduce it.

items: Proxy only the lab target.
Capture one known-good request.
Change one parameter or authorization context.
Observe status code, body, headers, and server-side evidence if available.
Repeat to confirm the result.

notes.text: Do not send destructive or resource-intensive payloads to systems outside the lab scope.

practicals.title: Authorization Test with Two Lab Accounts
practicals.description: Checks whether a user can access another user’s resource in an explicitly authorized test application.
steps: Create two distinct test accounts in the lab application.
Use account A to create or identify a resource owned by A.
Capture the request used to retrieve the resource.
Replay the request while authenticated as account B.
Record whether the application enforces object-level authorization.
practicals.solution: Use Burp Repeater or OWASP ZAP Replacer/Request Editor to replay the same request under the second authorized account. No payload is required; the security test is the authorization-context change.
practicals.output: Expected behavior is that account B is denied or receives a non-sensitive response when accessing account A’s protected resource.

quiz.question: What is the strongest evidence for an authorization issue?
options: A reproducible request showing a lower-privileged identity can access protected data
A long payload that caused no change
A generic statement that access control is important
quiz.answer: A reproducible request showing a lower-privileged identity can access protected data
quiz.explanation: Reproducibility plus a clear authorization context directly demonstrates the control failure.

summary: Proxy tooling is an observation and testing aid.
Authorization findings should prove who can access what under which identity.

lessons.title: Input Validation, Authentication and Session Review
lessons.description: Covers practical checks for server-side validation, authentication behavior, session handling, and safe error messages.
learningObjectives: Identify server-side validation requirements.
Review password and session handling at a control level.
Recognize authentication failures that warrant deeper investigation.

notes.text: Security validation belongs on the server because clients can be modified or bypassed. Authentication review includes credential policy, account recovery, lockout/rate limiting, and secure session lifecycle. The analyst should also check whether error responses reveal unnecessary implementation detail.

items: Prefer allowlists and type/range checks where the data domain is known.
Do not log passwords, authentication tokens, or secret material.
Session identifiers should be treated as secrets and protected in transit and at rest.

summary: Server-side validation is the enforcement boundary.
Authentication and session controls must be reviewed as a system, not as isolated fields.

tasks.title: Write a Reproducible Web Security Finding
tasks.description: Document a local-lab access-control flaw from evidence through remediation and regression test.
tasks.problemStatement: The application allows a second authorized user to retrieve another user’s record by changing an object identifier. Produce a finding that a developer can reproduce and fix.
objectives: State the authorization expectation.
Give the minimal reproduction steps.
Describe the observed response.
Recommend server-side object ownership checks.
Define a regression test.
tasks.hint: Focus on the authorization decision rather than the identifier itself; the server must derive the owner from the authenticated identity.
tasks.solutionCode:
Finding: Broken object-level authorization
Severity: Context-dependent; determine using asset sensitivity and exposure
Reproduction:
1. Authenticate as User A.
2. Retrieve resource R owned by A and record the request.
3. Authenticate as User B.
4. Repeat the same request with R.
Observed: User B receives R.
Fix: Load the requested resource with an ownership/authorization predicate bound to the authenticated principal.
Regression: Add an API test proving User B receives 403 or 404 for R.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution is deliberately framed around authorization logic, evidence, and regression testing. The identifier is not itself the vulnerability; the missing authorization decision is.

modules.title: Identity, Access, Cryptography and Secure Configuration
modules.description: Develops practical security administration skills around identity lifecycle, least privilege, authentication factors, password storage, cryptographic purpose, secrets handling, and zero-trust concepts.
objectives: Explain authentication, authorization, accounting, and least privilege.
Assess password and session controls at a defensive level.
Distinguish hashing, encryption, digital signatures, and key agreement.
Apply secure secret handling and configuration review.
Relate zero-trust principles to enterprise access decisions.

lessons.title: Identity Lifecycle, MFA and Least Privilege
lessons.description: Examines the lifecycle of identities from creation to deprovisioning and shows how permissions should be aligned to job responsibilities.
learningObjectives: Explain authentication versus authorization.
Design a simple joiner-mover-leaver checklist.
Identify excessive privilege and stale accounts.

notes.text: Identity security is not just a login screen. It includes account creation, role assignment, authentication factors, periodic review, privileged operations, and timely deprovisioning. Least privilege means granting only the access required for an approved task.

items: Create only the required identity.
Assign the narrowest role that meets the task.
Use stronger authentication for higher-risk access.
Review privilege changes and administrative actions.
Disable or remove access when no longer justified.
MFA adds an additional factor but does not eliminate phishing risk.
Shared privileged accounts reduce accountability and should be avoided where individual identities are practical.

quiz.question: Which principle most directly limits the blast radius of a compromised user account?
quiz.explanation: Least privilege constrains what the account can do even if its credentials are compromised.

summary: Authentication proves identity; authorization determines permitted actions.
Least privilege reduces impact when an identity is abused.

lessons.title: Password Storage, Sessions and Cryptographic Building Blocks
lessons.description: Explains common cryptographic primitives and what they are appropriate for in application and infrastructure security.
learningObjectives: Differentiate hashing and encryption.
Explain why passwords should use dedicated password-hashing algorithms rather than reversible encryption.
Describe the role of digital signatures and key agreement.

notes.text: Cryptographic functions have distinct purposes. Hashing provides a one-way transformation useful for integrity checks and password verification with dedicated password-hashing schemes. Encryption protects confidentiality. Digital signatures provide authenticity/integrity evidence tied to a private key. Key agreement establishes shared secrets for secure communication.
Do not invent your own cryptographic algorithm or password storage scheme. Use a well-established library and follow its documented secure usage.

items: Password storage should use a modern password-hashing function designed for passwords.
Session tokens should be unpredictable and protected like secrets.
Encryption without authenticated integrity can be insufficient for many application designs.

quiz.question: Which primitive is primarily intended to protect confidentiality?
quiz.explanation: Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext so that authorized parties can recover the content with the appropriate key.

summary: Cryptography is purpose-specific.
Secure password storage is not the same as encrypting passwords for later recovery.

lessons.title: Secrets, Secure Configuration and Zero Trust
lessons.description: Builds a practical configuration-review mindset: remove defaults, limit trust, protect secrets, and make access decisions close to the resource.
learningObjectives: Identify risky secret exposure patterns.
Apply configuration hardening principles.
Explain the core idea of zero trust as resource-focused access rather than implicit network trust.

notes.text: Secrets should not be embedded in source code or committed to repositories. Configuration should favor secure defaults, explicit exposure, and minimized privilege. NIST SP 800-207 describes zero trust as a shift away from implicit trust based solely on network location, with authentication and authorization performed before resource access.

export APP_SECRET="replace-with-a-secret-from-a-secret-manager"
# never commit the actual value to Git
git status --short

items: Use environment variables or dedicated secret-management systems where appropriate.
Remove default credentials from deployed systems.
Treat internal networks as untrusted for access decisions in zero-trust designs.

summary: Secrets belong outside source code and version history.
Zero trust focuses on protecting resources rather than trusting network location.

tasks.title: Audit a Secure Configuration Checklist
tasks.description: Review a lab service configuration for default credentials, unnecessary exposure, logging gaps, and privilege issues.
tasks.problemStatement: You are given a fictional but technically plausible server-hardening checklist. Mark controls as implemented, missing, not applicable, or requiring evidence.

modules.title: Threat Intelligence and Detection Engineering
modules.description: Develops the analyst skill of turning attacker behavior models and telemetry into defensible detections. The module uses MITRE ATT&CK, Sigma, Zeek, and Suricata as complementary references.
objectives: Use ATT&CK tactics and techniques to structure adversary-behavior hypotheses.
Identify appropriate data sources for a detection objective.
Write readable Sigma-style detections with clear field logic.
Interpret Zeek and Suricata telemetry at an analyst level.
Evaluate false-positive tradeoffs and detection coverage.

lessons.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Tactics, Techniques and Detection Thinking
lessons.description: Moves from “tool alert” thinking to behavior-based detection reasoning.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between tactics and techniques.
Map a security hypothesis to the telemetry it requires.
Use ATT&CK references without treating them as proof of an incident.

notes.text: ATT&CK tactics represent adversary goals (“why”), while techniques describe ways an adversary can achieve those goals (“how”). Detection strategies then organize high-level approaches for detecting techniques. An analyst should choose the data source that can actually observe the behavior of interest.

items: A technique mapping is a classification aid, not a verdict.
Detection quality depends on telemetry quality and environmental context.
MITRE data-source terminology is evolving; current detection strategy pages should be consulted for new work.

quiz.question: In ATT&CK terminology, what does a tactic represent?
options: The adversary’s goal or reason for an action
quiz.answer: The adversary’s goal or reason for an action
quiz.explanation: ATT&CK defines tactics as the “why” behind techniques.

summary: Use behavior models to choose telemetry and detections.
ATT&CK classifications help organize reasoning but do not prove maliciousness.

lessons.title: Sigma Detection Rules and Detection Logic
lessons.description: Teaches the structure of Sigma rules and how to avoid brittle or overly broad detections.
learningObjectives: Describe core Sigma rule fields.
Build a clear selection and condition.
Explain false positives and tuning.

notes.text: Sigma rules are YAML documents that describe detection logic in a backend-neutral way. Useful rules include a title, identifier, logsource, detection selection/condition, and metadata such as severity and references. The key engineering challenge is choosing fields and conditions that survive normal variation without generating excessive noise.

quiz.question: Why is a Sigma rule useful across multiple SIEM backends?
options: It expresses detection logic in a vendor-neutral format
It proves an alert is a confirmed incident
quiz.answer: It expresses detection logic in a vendor-neutral format
quiz.explanation: Sigma is designed as a generic signature/detection format that can be converted for supported backends.

summary: Detection logic should be explicit and testable.
Tuning is part of detection engineering, not an afterthought.

lessons.title: Zeek, Suricata and Telemetry Correlation
lessons.description: Shows how network telemetry can identify unusual behavior and how multiple data sources can be correlated before escalation.
learningObjectives: Interpret common Zeek logs such as conn.log, dns.log, and http.log.
Explain the role of Suricata signatures and EVE JSON.
Correlate network events with identity or endpoint context.

notes.text: Zeek is a passive network traffic analyzer that produces structured logs describing connections and application-layer activity. Suricata is an IDS/IPS and network security engine with rule-based detection and structured event output. The strongest analyst conclusions often come from correlation rather than a single network record.

items: Zeek conn.log can establish who talked to whom and when.
Zeek dns.log can reveal name-resolution behavior and failures.
Suricata alerts can provide a detection signal that should be validated with context.

modules.title: Incident Response and Digital Forensic Reasoning
modules.description: Builds an evidence-driven response workflow aligned with current NIST incident-response guidance, including preparation, analysis, containment, recovery, evidence preservation, timeline reasoning, and post-incident improvement.
objectives: Explain incident response within the NIST CSF 2.0 risk-management context.
Build an incident timeline from mixed evidence.
Differentiate triage facts from hypotheses.
Preserve evidence and document handling decisions.
Write containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons-learned actions.

lessons.title: Incident Response Lifecycle and Triage
lessons.description: Introduces current NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 guidance and shows how response work fits throughout cybersecurity risk management.
learningObjectives: Explain the current status of NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3.
Separate preparation, detection/analysis, response, and recovery concerns.
Create a triage checklist for a suspected compromise.

notes.text: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 was finalized in April 2025 and supersedes Rev. 2. The document positions incident response within CSF 2.0 cybersecurity risk management rather than as a standalone after-the-fact process.

items: Establish what happened and what is known.
Scope affected systems and identities.
Preserve evidence and avoid destructive actions.
Contain based on risk and operational needs.
Eradicate the cause when understood.
Recover and monitor for recurrence.
Capture lessons learned and control improvements.

quiz.question: Which NIST incident-response publication is the current revision and supersedes SP 800-61 Rev. 2?

summary: Incident response is integrated into broader risk management.

lessons.title: Timeline Analysis and Evidence Handling
lessons.description: Teaches how to build a coherent timeline from logs, network records, and host artifacts while maintaining provenance.
learningObjectives: Normalize timestamps and time zones.
Build a timeline from heterogeneous evidence.
Record provenance and integrity metadata.

notes.text: Timeline analysis is powerful because many security events are only meaningful in sequence. Analysts should normalize timestamps, preserve the original source time, and record which artifact produced each event.

sha256sum evidence/*.log
stat evidence/suspect.log
python - <<'PY'

for p in sorted(Path("evidence").glob("*.log")):
    print(p.name, p.stat().st_size)
PY

items: Preserve originals whenever possible.
Hash exported evidence so later changes can be detected.
Do not infer an event solely from file timestamps when stronger evidence exists.

lessons.title: Containment, Recovery and Reporting
lessons.description: Shows how technical response actions become coordinated incident work products.

Write recovery verification criteria.

Eradication should address the enabling condition, not just the symptom.
Recovery should include validation and monitoring for recurrence.
Lessons learned should become control, detection, process, or training improvements.
Do not fabricate attacker identity or attribution.

Document who authorized major containment actions.

project.heading: Build a Defensive Security Operations Triage Toolkit
project.description: Build a local, defensive security-triage application for a small analyst team. The toolkit accepts synthetic or explicitly authorized JSONL security events, normalizes them into stable event objects, evaluates readable detection rules, enriches matched events with exact indicators of compromise, assigns a transparent triage score, stores alerts and case metadata in SQLite, and exports analyst-friendly reports. The project is relevant because it forces the intern to combine security reasoning with implementation, evidence handling, testing, secure configuration, and documentation. It is deliberately a lab-grade prototype, not a production SIEM.
project.problemStatement: A small security team receives heterogeneous authentication and network events but lacks a lightweight way to normalize them, apply repeatable detections, enrich indicators, retain alert evidence, and export a reviewable triage report. Build a self-contained defensive toolkit that makes those decisions explicit and testable while remaining safe for a local training environment.
objectives: Implement a complete event-to-alert pipeline.
Apply detection rules and exact IOC enrichment.
Persist alerts safely using parameterized SQL.
Provide CLI commands for ingestion and reporting.
Write automated tests covering parsing, rules, IOC matching, and the end-to-end pipeline.
Document security assumptions, limitations, and safe operating boundaries.

functional: Read JSONL events with timezone-aware timestamps.
Reject malformed JSON and timestamps without time-zone information.
Evaluate equality, containment, membership, regular-expression, and numeric comparison operators.
Load exact IOCs for IPs, domains, and SHA-256 values.
Create enriched alerts with reason, severity, and transparent score.
Persist alerts and incident-case metadata in SQLite.
Export alert records to JSON or CSV.
technical: Standard-library implementation for core application logic.
security: Treat event files and rule files as untrusted inputs.
Avoid logging complete sensitive event payloads.
Restrict operation to synthetic or explicitly authorized data.
testing: Unit tests for timestamp parsing and rule operators.
IOC matching tests including case/trailing-dot domain normalization.
End-to-end persistence test using in-memory SQLite.
deployment: Local virtual environment is the reference deployment. Optional containerization may be explored only after the base application works.

features: Timezone-aware JSONL event normalization that preserves original fields for evidence.
Deterministic detection rules with explicit field/operator/condition semantics.
Exact IOC matching for IPv4-address values, normalized domains, and SHA-256 values.
Transparent triage scoring with separate severity and enrichment inputs.
SQLite-backed alert storage using parameterized SQL and foreign-key enforcement.
JSON and CSV report export for analyst review.
Automated tests for the security-critical transformation and persistence path.
Explicit safety and limitation documentation for controlled training use.

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from typing import Any


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Event:

    event_type: str
    source: str
    fields: dict[str, Any]

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

from .models import Alert, Case

SCHEMA = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS alerts (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    rule_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    rule_name TEXT NOT NULL,
    severity TEXT NOT NULL,
    score INTEGER NOT NULL,
    timestamp TEXT NOT NULL,
    event_type TEXT NOT NULL,
    source TEXT NOT NULL,
    reason TEXT NOT NULL,
    evidence_json TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cases (
    case_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    priority TEXT NOT NULL,
    notes_json TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS case_alerts (
    case_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    alert_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (case_id, alert_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (case_id) REFERENCES cases(case_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (alert_id) REFERENCES alerts(id)
);
"""


def connect(path: str | Path) -> sqlite3.Connection:
    conn = sqlite3.connect(path)
    conn.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
    conn.executescript(SCHEMA)
    return conn


def insert_alert(conn: sqlite3.Connection, alert: Alert) -> int:
    cursor = conn.execute(
        "INSERT INTO alerts (rule_id, rule_name, severity, score, timestamp, event_type, source, reason, evidence_json) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
        (alert.rule_id, alert.rule_name, alert.severity, alert.score, alert.timestamp.isoformat(), alert.event_type, alert.source, alert.reason, json.dumps(alert.evidence, sort_keys=True)),
    )
    conn.commit()
    return int(cursor.lastrowid)


def insert_case(conn: sqlite3.Connection, case: Case) -> None:
    conn.execute(
        "INSERT INTO cases (case_id, title, status, priority, notes_json) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
        (case.case_id, case.title, case.status, case.priority, json.dumps(case.notes)),
    )
    conn.commit()


def attach_alert(conn: sqlite3.Connection, case_id: str, alert_id: int) -> None:
    conn.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO case_alerts (case_id, alert_id) VALUES (?, ?)", (case_id, alert_id))
    conn.commit()


def list_alerts(conn: sqlite3.Connection) -> list[dict]:
    rows = conn.execute("SELECT id, rule_id, rule_name, severity, score, timestamp, event_type, source, reason FROM alerts ORDER BY score DESC, timestamp DESC").fetchall()
    columns = [d[0] for d in conn.execute("SELECT id, rule_id, rule_name, severity, score, timestamp, event_type, source, reason FROM alerts LIMIT 0").description]
    return [dict(zip(columns, row)) for row in rows]

fileWiseSolution.purpose: Ingest events, apply rules, match IOCs, score alerts, and persist results
fileWiseSolution.explanation: This is the main analyst workflow: normalize -> detect -> enrich -> score -> persist. Each step is explicit so the intern can debug it independently.
fileWiseSolution.code:
from __future__ import annotations

from .db import insert_alert
from .ioc import IOCSet, match_iocs
from .models import Alert, Event, Rule
from .rules import rule_matches
from .scorer import score


def process_events(events: list[Event], rules: list[Rule], iocs: IOCSet, conn) -> list[int]:
    alert_ids: list[int] = []
    for event in sorted(events, key=lambda item: item.timestamp):
        for rule in rules:
            matched, reason = rule_matches(event, rule)
            if not matched:
                continue
            ioc_hits = match_iocs(event, iocs)
            auth_failure = event.event_type == "authentication" and event.fields.get("outcome") == "failure"
            alert_score = score(rule.severity, len(ioc_hits), auth_failure)
            if ioc_hits:
                reason = f"{reason}; IOC matches: {', '.join(ioc_hits)}"
            alert = Alert(
                rule_id=rule.rule_id,
                rule_name=rule.name,
                severity=rule.severity,
                score=alert_score,
                timestamp=event.timestamp,
                event_type=event.event_type,
                source=event.source,
                reason=reason,
                evidence=event.fields,
            )
            alert_ids.append(insert_alert(conn, alert))
    return alert_ids

from __future__ import annotations

import csv
import json
from pathlib import Path

def export_json(rows: list[dict], path: str | Path) -> None:
    Path(path).write_text(json.dumps(rows, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

def export_csv(rows: list[dict], path: str | Path) -> None:
    if not rows:
        Path(path).write_text("", encoding="utf-8")
        return
    with Path(path).open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(handle, fieldnames=rows[0].keys())
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(rows)

    report.add_argument("--db", required=True)
    report.add_argument("--format", choices=["json", "csv"], required=True)
    report.add_argument("--output", required=True)
    return parser


def main() -> None:
    configure()
    args = build_parser().parse_args()
    if args.command == "ingest":
        events = list(load_jsonl(args.events))
        rules = load_rules(args.rules)
        iocs = load_iocs(args.iocs)
        conn = connect(args.db)
        ids = process_events(events, rules, iocs, conn)
        print(f"created_alerts={len(ids)}")
        return
    if args.command == "report":
        conn = connect(args.db)
        rows = list_alerts(conn)
        if args.format == "json":
            export_json(rows, args.output)
        else:
            export_csv(rows, args.output)
        print(f"exported_rows={len(rows)}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from datetime import datetime, timezone

from secops_triage.db import connect, list_alerts
from secops_triage.ioc import IOCSet
from secops_triage.models import Condition, Event, Rule
from secops_triage.pipeline import process_events


def test_pipeline_creates_alerts():
    conn = connect(":memory:")
    event = Event(datetime(2026,9,7,9,tzinfo=timezone.utc), "network", "zeek", {"dst_ip":"203.0.113.55"})
    rule = Rule("NET-1", "Network IOC Candidate", "high", (Condition("event_type", "eq", "network"),))
    iocs = IOCSet(frozenset({"203.0.113.55"}), frozenset(), frozenset())
    ids = process_events([event], [rule], iocs, conn)
    assert len(ids) == 1
    rows = list_alerts(conn)
    assert rows[0]["severity"] == "high"
    assert rows[0]["score"] >= 7

fileWiseSolution.code:
# Security Operations Triage Toolkit

## Purpose
This project is a controlled defensive-security lab. It ingests synthetic JSONL security events, applies explicit detection rules, enriches matches with a small IOC set, stores alerts in SQLite, and exports analyst reports.

## Safety boundary
Use the toolkit only with synthetic or explicitly authorized data. Do not ingest personal credentials, access tokens, private keys, or unnecessary personal data.

## Setup

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .
pip install -e ".[test]"
```

## Ingest

```bash
secops-triage ingest \
  --events data/events.example.jsonl \
  --rules rules/authentication.json \
  --iocs data/iocs.example.csv \
  --db triage.sqlite3
```

## Export

```bash
secops-triage report --db triage.sqlite3 --format json --output alerts.json
secops-triage report --db triage.sqlite3 --format csv --output alerts.csv
```

## Tests

```bash
python -m pytest -q
```

## Analyst workflow
1. Confirm evidence source and scope.
2. Ingest and normalize events.
3. Review rule matches and IOC enrichment.
4. Examine score and reason, not score alone.
5. Validate the alert against host/network context.
6. Create or update an incident case when evidence supports escalation.
7. Export and document the investigation.

## Limitations
This is a training toolkit, not a production SIEM, EDR, SOAR, or incident-response platform. It does not implement multi-user authorization, distributed ingestion, tamper-evident storage, or live packet collection.

project.howItWorks: At startup the CLI parses the command and configures logging. For `ingest`, the JSONL loader reads one record at a time. The normalizer validates timezone-aware timestamps and creates immutable Event objects. The rule engine evaluates each configured Rule against the event. If a rule matches, the IOC matcher checks exact IP/domain/hash indicators and the scorer calculates a transparent triage score from configured severity plus enrichment signals. The persistence layer inserts the alert with parameterized SQL into SQLite. The report command queries stored alerts and serializes them as JSON or CSV. Tests exercise each security-sensitive transformation and the end-to-end alert path.

testing.expectedOutcome: Tests should complete successfully in an environment where pytest is installed. No fabricated numeric test result is stated in the internship content.

securityReview: SQL statements use placeholders rather than string concatenation.
Imported JSON and IOC files are parsed with explicit validation.
Unsupported operators and IOC types produce errors instead of being silently accepted.
No application secret is embedded in source code.
Logging is intentionally minimal and avoids serializing event payloads by default.
Domain normalization is exact rather than substring-based to reduce false matches.
The project is restricted to synthetic or explicitly authorized data.
The project is documented as a lab-grade prototype rather than a production SIEM.
performanceReview: Events are processed sequentially to keep reasoning simple and deterministic.
The sample project is intended for local training data, not high-volume production ingestion.
For larger datasets, measure runtime and memory before introducing batching, streaming backpressure, indexing strategy, or parallel processing.
deploymentGuidance: Run locally in a dedicated virtual environment.
Keep the SQLite database and evidence directory protected by appropriate filesystem permissions.
Use a read-only sample-data directory for training inputs where practical.
For any production evolution, replace local persistence and simple scoring with organization-approved architectures, controls, and threat models.
troubleshooting: If timestamps fail, confirm that they include an explicit UTC offset or Z suffix.
If no alerts appear, inspect the event schema and rule field names before changing the rule logic.
If IOC matches do not appear, verify exact value normalization and IOC type labels.
If SQLite inserts fail, inspect the database file permissions and schema initialization path.
If tests cannot import the package, ensure `tests/conftest.py` is present or install the package in editable mode.
project.finalProjectExplanation: The project demonstrates a complete defensive-security workflow rather than a collection of isolated scripts. The design forces the intern to define an observation boundary, normalize untrusted input, encode detection logic explicitly, enrich findings with indicators, persist evidence safely, and produce reviewable outputs. Its most important engineering lesson is the separation between an automated signal and a confirmed security incident: the toolkit generates alerts, while a human analyst must validate scope, context, evidence quality, and business impact before escalation.
